lesson_title: Rust: The Slow Fire Eating Our Cars
hook_text: Rust is fire in slow motion. And at the coast it burns a lot faster.
clip_script: Rust is iron burning in slow motion. Steel wool grabs oxygen in seconds and sparkles; a gate left out in the rain does the same thing over years. But rust needs two things together, air and water. Take away either and iron stays shiny. Prove it with three nails. One in water open to the air: rusty. One in boiled water under a layer of oil, with no air: shiny. One in dry air with a drying chemical: shiny. Add salt and it rusts fastest of all, which is why cars in Durban rust long before cars in the Karoo. Rust flakes off and exposes fresh iron, so it keeps eating inwards. To stop it, keep air and water out with paint, oil or plastic. Or plate it with shiny chromium. Or coat it in zinc, a bodyguard that sacrifices itself, so even a scratch stays rust-free.
visual_style: Time-lapse of a nail turning orange; three labelled test tubes side by side; a coastal bakkie with rust holes; a zinc-coated roof with a scratch staying silver.
pacing: Hook with the slow-fire idea, brisk three-tube reveal, a punchy list of defences.
